def: The course's own four-part check — independence, read or write, specifiability, and value against roughly ten times the tokens — used to decide whether a task should be split across agents.
deeper: This is a synthesis assembled by the course, not a rule from any single source: question one comes from the documented boundary that domains with 'many dependencies between agents are not a good fit for multi-agent systems today', and question four from 'multi-agent systems require tasks where the value of the task is high enough to pay for the increased performance'.[^S1] Treat it as a decision aid whose parts are sourced, not as a validated instrument.
pitfall: Treating a yes on question four as sufficient, so any high-value task gets split regardless of whether its pieces are independent. Value justifies the cost of splitting; it never creates the independence that makes splitting work.
distractor_rationale: People arrive at this course because a task felt too big, and 'too big' is a statement about value and effort. The first three questions ask about structure, which is a different property, and the habit of reasoning about importance carries over.

def: The ratio of tokens a multi-agent run consumes against a single conversation on the same class of task.
deeper: The published figures are that agents 'typically use about 4x more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15x more tokens than chats'.[^S1] A separate build comparison put a solo run at about 9 dollars and a three-agent harness at about 200 dollars on the same prompt, which is a different ratio again on a different task shape.[^S6]
pitfall: Quoting a figure like fifteen times as a constant. It was measured on one vendor's search-heavy research workload; a fan-out of three short read-only workers costs far less, and a long autonomous build can cost far more.
distractor_rationale: A single memorable number is easier to carry than a range with a setting attached, and the number gets repeated in secondary write-ups stripped of the workload it came from.

def: A benchmark built and run by the organisation reporting the result, against its own task distribution.
pitfall: Reading a large internal-eval gain as a general capability claim. The 90.2% figure is on Anthropic's own research eval for breadth-first search queries, and the same post says most coding tasks do not have that shape.
distractor_rationale: The number is precise to one decimal place and published by a credible engineering team, which reads as rigour. Precision describes the measurement, not how far the result travels.

def: A task shape where several independent directions can be pursued at once, with no direction depending on another's findings.
deeper: The documented gain is scoped to this shape: multi-agent research systems 'excel especially for breadth-first queries that involve pursuing multiple independent directions simultaneously'.[^S1] The same post names the counter-case, where domains 'require all agents to share the same context or involve many dependencies between agents'.[^S1]
pitfall: Assuming a task is breadth-first because it has many pieces. Forty files to migrate has many pieces and one shared convention, which makes it a single job with forty locations rather than forty directions.
distractor_rationale: Breadth is visible from the outside as a count of items, while the dependency that collapses it is a convention nobody has written down yet — so the surface reading is always the available one.

def: The choices an agent makes while working that it never states — what counted as in scope, which pattern to follow, how to read an ambiguous instruction.
deeper: The principle as stated: 'Actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting decisions carry bad results.'[^S3] The illustration is two workers producing a bird and a background 'with completely different visual styles' because their 'actions were based on conflicting assumptions not prescribed upfront'.[^S3] This is a vendor engineering blog arguing a position rather than reporting a measurement.
pitfall: Believing that copying the full original task into every worker's brief removes them. It reduces divergence about the goal and does nothing about the hundreds of small choices each worker makes while working, which is where incompatibility actually originates.
distractor_rationale: The failure looks like a communication problem, and communication problems are usually fixed by sending more information. Here the information does not exist to send: the decisions are made after the brief and are never surfaced by the worker.

def: One agent working through a task in one continuous context, with no delegation.
deeper: Cognition's recommendation is direct: 'The simplest way to follow the principles is to just use a single-threaded linear agent.'[^S3] Anthropic's older patterns essay reaches the same default from another direction: 'find the simplest solution possible, and only increasing complexity when needed'.[^S2]
pitfall: Dismissing it as the naive option that this course exists to replace. It is the recommended default in the strongest published critique of multi-agent architectures, and the honest end state of many first end-to-end comparisons.
distractor_rationale: Having learned the machinery of orchestration, using none of it feels like not applying the lesson. The lesson includes knowing when it does not apply.

def: The Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy: fourteen failure modes in three categories, derived from annotated execution traces of open-source multi-agent frameworks.
deeper: Built from 'MAST-Data, a comprehensive dataset of 1600+ annotated traces collected across 7 popular MAS frameworks', with the taxonomy developed from 150 traces at 'high inter-annotator agreement (kappa = 0.88)'.[^S4] Its central claim is that failures arise from 'organizational design and agent coordination rather than the limitations of individual agents'.[^S4]
pitfall: Reading its prevalence percentages as rates for a current commercial coding agent. The traces come from research frameworks such as MetaGPT, ChatDev and AG2 on GPT-4-era and Claude-3-era models; the categories generalise, the numbers describe that population.
distractor_rationale: The study is peer-reviewed with a stated inter-annotator agreement, so its numbers look like the most rigorous available — and they are, for what they measured. The gap is between what was measured and the tool on your machine today.

def: A worker redoing work that has already been done elsewhere in the system, recorded as the single most common failure mode in the MAST trace population at 15.7%.
pitfall: Treating it as wasted tokens only. Two workers repeating a step produce two independent answers to the same question, and when those answers differ the synthesiser has a contradiction with no way to resolve it.
distractor_rationale: Repetition reads as an efficiency problem because the visible symptom is duplicated effort. The correctness consequence appears one layer later, in the synthesis, where it is no longer recognisable as repetition.

def: The constraint that output produced in parallel must still be read serially by a person, so review capacity rather than machine throughput sets the useful rate.
deeper: Stated by a practitioner reporting his own workflow rather than a measurement: 'AI-generated code needs to be reviewed, which means the natural bottleneck on all of this is how fast I can review the results.'[^S12] His resolution is to parallelise work that does not queue for review — research, small maintenance, and work built from a specification he wrote himself.[^S12]
pitfall: Measuring a fan-out's benefit in run time alone. A wave that finishes in four minutes and takes forty minutes to review saved far less than the run-time comparison suggests, and unreviewed output is not a result.
distractor_rationale: Run time is the number the tool reports and review time is the number nobody records, so the comparison people make is between the figure they have and the figure they remember from the serial case.

def: A file holding a decision that every worker must follow identically — a schema, a specification, an interface — written before dispatch so the decision is made once rather than per worker.
pitfall: Trying to carry the decision in the briefs instead. Ten briefs describing the same convention in prose produce ten readings of it; one file that every worker reads produces one.
distractor_rationale: A brief is the obvious channel because it is the one the tooling gives you, and putting the convention there feels like thoroughness rather than like a per-worker reinterpretation.

def: A shared choice that has no single right answer but must be the same everywhere — a field name, an error shape, a naming pattern.
pitfall: Assuming a convention exists because the codebase has one. Unless it is written somewhere a worker will read, each worker infers it from whatever it happens to look at, and different samples yield different inferences.
distractor_rationale: In a repository with reasonably consistent code, the convention feels like a property of the code rather than knowledge held by the people maintaining it — right up until several workers each derive their own version.

def: Work that mostly reads and reports rather than modifying anything, and the documented starting point for parallel dispatch.
deeper: The guidance is explicit: 'use parallel agents for read-heavy tasks such as exploration, tests, triage, and summarization. Be more careful with parallel write-heavy workflows, because agents editing code at once can create conflicts and increase coordination overhead.'[^S9]
pitfall: Classifying work as read-heavy because most of it is reading. One write at the end makes the whole task a writing task for dispatch purposes, since that write is where conflicts and unreviewable changes appear.
distractor_rationale: The proportion of reading really is high in most audit or survey tasks, so the label fits the effort distribution while missing the thing that determines risk.

def: An arrangement in which one lead agent holds the plan, delegates pieces to workers, receives their results, and decides when the work is done.
deeper: The published description: 'a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel.'[^S1] A distinct arrangement exists where peers 'communicate directly with each other' and coordinate through a shared task list rather than through a lead, at higher cost since 'each teammate is a separate Claude instance'.[^S8]
pitfall: Assuming the workers can see each other. Every message travels through the lead, so two workers' incompatible assumptions are invisible until their reports arrive together.
distractor_rationale: Diagrams of the pattern show the workers side by side, which reads as a team. Adjacency on a diagram is not a channel.

def: The agent that analyses the task, decides how many workers to create and what each does, receives their reports, and judges whether the work is complete.
pitfall: Expecting the lead to notice that two workers disagreed. It sees only what the reports say, so a disagreement produced by different unstated definitions arrives as two plain statements with no marker on either.
distractor_rationale: The lead is the only component with the whole picture, which makes it feel like the place where discrepancies would surface. It has the whole picture of the reports, not of the work.

def: An agent given one piece of a decomposed task, running in its own context, reporting back to the lead.
pitfall: Assuming a worker knows anything about the project beyond its brief. It starts fresh: no conversation history, no files already read, no decisions from your session.
distractor_rationale: Workers run inside your tool and against your repository, so it feels like they share your situation. They share the filesystem and nothing else.

def: The message that constitutes a worker's entire knowledge of the task: objective, output format, sources, and boundaries.
deeper: The four required parts are documented from experience: 'Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries. Without detailed task descriptions, agents duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information.'[^S1]
pitfall: Writing it in the vocabulary of your own session. Phrases like 'the new format' or 'as we discussed' resolve for you and are blanks the worker fills silently.
distractor_rationale: The brief is written immediately after a stretch of work in which those phrases had clear referents, so their ambiguity is genuinely invisible to the person writing.

def: The part of a brief naming the specific question this worker answers, precise enough that an adjacent question cannot be substituted for it.
pitfall: Naming a topic instead of a question. 'Look at error handling in module X' is a topic, and three workers given it will inventory three different things, all responsive and none comparable.
distractor_rationale: A topic feels like it leaves room for the worker to find what matters, which is a virtue in exploratory work with one agent and a defect when several outputs must line up.

def: The named fields a worker's report must contain, fixed before dispatch so several reports can be read against each other.
deeper: The documented requirement covers three things: a dispatch 'should explain how to divide the work, whether Codex should wait for all agents before continuing, and what summary or output to return'.[^S9] The complementary recommendation is to 'Return summaries from subagents instead of raw intermediate output.'[^S9]
pitfall: Omitting a field you will want later. A field you did not ask for is a field you will not get, and asking afterwards means running the worker again from a context that no longer exists.
distractor_rationale: During briefing, the fields that matter seem obvious and few; the ones you end up needing are the ones that only become interesting once several reports are side by side.

def: The part of a brief stating where this worker's job ends — both what it must not do and where the next worker's territory begins.
pitfall: Writing only the prohibitions. Negative boundaries stop damage; the positive boundary, saying where this piece ends, is what stops two workers covering the same ground.
distractor_rationale: Prohibitions are the boundaries that come to mind because they are the ones with a visible consequence. Overlap has no visible consequence at dispatch time, only a cost at synthesis.

def: Two or more workers independently covering the same ground because the division between them was never stated.
deeper: The documented instance: 'one subagent explored the 2021 automotive chip crisis while 2 others duplicated work investigating current 2025 supply chains, without an effective division of labor.'[^S1]
pitfall: Assuming it announces itself. Overlapping reports look like corroboration, and two workers reaching the same conclusion feels like confirmation rather than like paying twice for one answer.
distractor_rationale: Independent agreement is genuinely evidence in most contexts. It is not here, because both workers ran the same procedure over the same material rather than reaching the same place by different routes.

def: Explicit guidance on how many workers and how much effort a task class warrants, written into the lead's instructions rather than left to its judgment.
deeper: The published tiering: 'Simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities.'[^S1] The rules exist because early versions were 'spawning 50 subagents for simple queries'.[^S1] The tool-call counts belong to a web-research workload.
pitfall: Scaling the worker count without scaling the division of labour. Ten workers on work that divides cleanly five ways is five workers plus five sources of overlap.
distractor_rationale: Worker count is the visible dial, so it is the one people turn. The division of responsibilities is the actual constraint and it is not represented by any number in the interface.

def: A decomposition where you enumerate the subtasks yourself and dispatch them, because you already know what the pieces are.
pitfall: Handing the split to the model when you could enumerate it. That adds a step that can go wrong and buys flexibility you do not need.
distractor_rationale: Letting the orchestrator decide feels more capable, and more like what an orchestration system is for. The published distinction is about your knowledge, not about sophistication.

def: A decomposition where a central model determines the subtasks at run time from the specific input, because they cannot be predicted in advance.
deeper: The distinction as published: 'a central LLM dynamically breaks down tasks, delegates them to worker LLMs, and synthesizes their results... the key difference from parallelization is its flexibility - subtasks aren't pre-defined, but determined by the orchestrator based on the specific input.'[^S2] That essay is from December 2024 and is cited for the distinction, not for current tooling behaviour.
pitfall: Using it for work whose pieces you could have listed. The flexibility has a cost — a decomposition step whose output you did not review — and it is only worth paying when enumeration is genuinely impossible.
distractor_rationale: The two shapes look identical as diagrams, so the choice appears cosmetic. It is a choice about who makes the decomposition decision and whether anyone checks it.

def: The composed summary of a task that a lead sends to a fresh worker, and the only thing that crosses into the worker's context.
deeper: The mechanism: 'Each subagent starts with a fresh, isolated context window. It doesn't see your conversation history, the skills you've already invoked, or the files Claude has already read. Claude composes a delegation message that summarizes the task, and the subagent works from there.'[^S7]
pitfall: Treating difficulty writing it as a prompting problem to push through. The effort of reconstructing your session in the message is the measurement of coupling, arriving before you pay for the split.
distractor_rationale: Every other prompting difficulty in agent work does yield to more careful writing, so the reflex is to keep rewriting. Here the length of the rewrite is the signal.

def: A worker's own context, holding its system prompt, its brief, and everything it reads — none of which is visible to the lead, and none of which survives the worker.
pitfall: Thinking of it as a private copy of your session. It is a separate session that shares your filesystem and nothing else, so anything not in the brief is genuinely absent.
distractor_rationale: Isolation sounds like a filter on something shared. Here there was never anything shared to filter.

def: The narrow path a worker's findings take back to the lead: a condensed summary, not a transcript.
deeper: The published ratio: 'Each subagent might explore extensively, using tens of thousands of tokens or more, but returns only a condensed, distilled summary of its work (often 1,000-2,000 tokens).'[^S1] The figure describes typical returns on one research workload rather than a limit.
pitfall: Reading the narrowness as a limitation to work around. It is the mechanism that makes the architecture worth its cost — transcripts returning in full would refill the lead's window with exactly what the split was meant to keep out.
distractor_rationale: Every other part of the system rewards more information, so a channel that deliberately discards most of it reads as a constraint imposed by the tooling rather than as the design.

def: The reduction of a worker's whole context into a report, performed in one pass by the same agent whose work is being described.
deeper: Cognition describes building a component for exactly this and found it 'hard to get right', to the point of fine-tuning a smaller model for the job.[^S3] Every worker summary you receive is that problem solved in one untuned pass.
pitfall: Assuming it preserves the important parts and drops detail. What survives is the conclusions; what disappears is the reasoning, the scope choices, and everything the worker failed to find.
distractor_rationale: Summarising well is a familiar human skill with a familiar failure mode — losing nuance — so people expect a degraded version of the same thing rather than a different selection.

def: Roughly how much a worker consumed against how much it returned — the only available signal for how much unseen judgment stands behind a report.
pitfall: Ignoring it because two reports look the same on screen. A worker that read four files and one that read four hundred can produce identical-looking pages, and only one of them made hundreds of invisible relevance decisions.
distractor_rationale: The report is the artifact in front of you and the consumption is a number in a log, if it is recorded at all — so the available evidence is the one that says nothing about trustworthiness.

def: A worker's private determinations about what counted as in or out of its task — what a handler is, whether generated code was included, where the module ends.
pitfall: Expecting them in the report. They are not there unless the format made a slot for them, and each one silently narrows or widens what the findings actually cover.
distractor_rationale: The report answers the question you asked, which makes it feel complete. The scope over which it answered is a separate fact that no field carries by default.

def: The class of information a worker did not locate, whose absence in a report is indistinguishable from a genuine negative finding.
deeper: The measured population supports treating this as structural: in the MAST traces, 'no or incomplete verification' appeared in 8.2% and 'incorrect verification' in 9.1%.[^S4] Those figures describe research frameworks on older models rather than any current tool.
pitfall: Reading 'no X found' as 'there is no X'. A worker that searched two directories and one that searched the whole repository write the same sentence.
distractor_rationale: A negative finding is a legitimate result and reads like one. Nothing in the sentence carries information about the search behind it, and no reader is prompted to ask.

def: The report entry a worker uses for something it could not resolve, together with what it would need to resolve it.
pitfall: Reading undetermined entries as a failed run. They are the best outcome available for a gap: a gap that announced itself instead of being absorbed into an agreement it never joined.
distractor_rationale: Every other field returns a finding, so a field returning a non-answer looks like the worker underperforming rather than like the format doing its job.

def: A named place in the output format where a worker puts what it could not determine, created before the run because uncertainty with nowhere to go becomes silence.
pitfall: Adding it after seeing a suspicious report. By then the worker's context is gone, and the only way to get the field is to run the task again.
distractor_rationale: It looks like a formatting detail that can be tightened iteratively, the way most output requirements can. This one cannot, because the information it captures is destroyed when the worker ends.

def: An output field carrying a path and line for every claim, so a finding can be checked without re-running the worker.
pitfall: Treating the references as exact citations. They are locators produced from a context you cannot inspect, and spot-checks routinely find them pointing at the right file and the wrong line.
distractor_rationale: A path with a line number has the form of a precise citation, and in code review that form usually is precise because a human or a tool generated it from the file directly.

def: Any reference in a report that lets a reader find the underlying evidence themselves — a path, a line, an identifier, a command to run.
pitfall: Leaving it out of negative findings. A claim that something is absent has no natural location, which makes it the one claim in a report that cannot be checked and the one most worth checking.
distractor_rationale: Locators feel like a courtesy attached to positive findings, since that is where they have an obvious target. The asymmetry is exactly why negative claims slip through unexamined.

def: Fidelity loss as a result passes through intermediate agents, each restating rather than forwarding it.
deeper: The documented workaround: 'Subagents call tools to store their work in external systems, then pass lightweight references back to the coordinator. This prevents information loss during multi-stage processing and reduces token overhead from copying large outputs through conversation history.'[^S1] The same file-based pattern appears in a three-agent harness where 'Communication was handled via files'.[^S6]
pitfall: Accepting it for deliverables. Findings survive restatement; a generated file, a full extract, or a long list is destroyed by it and should be written to disk with a reference returned instead.
distractor_rationale: The compression that makes findings affordable applies uniformly by default, so outputs whose value lies in their exact content get the same treatment as outputs whose value is their conclusion.

def: The common name for a worker agent spawned by another agent, running with its own context window, tools, and permissions.
pitfall: Reading the term as a smaller or weaker agent. It is the same kind of agent in a different position, and its context window is sized by its own model rather than by the parent's.
distractor_rationale: The 'sub' prefix suggests a reduced version, and in most software hierarchies a sub-component is genuinely lesser. Here it names a relationship, not a capability level.

def: The map of which pieces of a task need which other pieces' output, drawn before any dispatch decision.
deeper: The documented consequence: agent teams 'work best when teammates can operate independently. For sequential tasks, same-file edits, or work with many dependencies, a single session or subagents are more effective.'[^S8]
pitfall: Confusing a preference for an order with a real dependency, or the reverse. 'We should probably do the schema first' is usually a stage boundary wearing a suggestion's clothing.
distractor_rationale: Dependencies that flow as data are easy to see. Dependencies that flow as a shared convention have no visible arrow, and are the ones that break a fan-out.

def: A relationship where no piece needs another's result, so all of them can run at once.
pitfall: Testing for independence by asking whether the pieces touch each other. The better test is what each worker would have to invent on its own, and whether two different inventions would be visible to you.
distractor_rationale: Non-interaction is observable from the task description and shared assumptions are not, so the available test is the one that misses the failure.

def: A relationship where each step's result determines what the next step should be, so concurrency cannot help.
pitfall: Dispatching several workers on a sequential task to explore in parallel. Each one works from the picture available at dispatch, which the first finding already made obsolete.
distractor_rationale: Parallel exploration is a real pattern for testing competing hypotheses, so it feels applicable. It requires hypotheses, and at the start of a sequential investigation there are none.

def: A structure of independent groups separated by points where everything must converge before the next group starts.
pitfall: Flattening it. Ten pieces across two stages look like ten pieces, and dispatching them together means the second stage runs before the decision it depends on exists.
distractor_rationale: From a distance the piece count is the salient number, and the convergence point is a single moment with no representation in a list of tasks.

def: The point in a staged task where work must converge — a decision made, an artifact written — before any later piece can start.
pitfall: Believing a bigger fan-out can dissolve one. It cannot: what the boundary marks is a decision that has to exist before the work depending on it, and concurrency does not create decisions.
distractor_rationale: Most bottlenecks in computing do yield to more parallelism, so the habit is to add workers. This bottleneck is informational rather than throughput-bound.

def: The property of a task that can genuinely be split into pieces workers can hold separately, as distinct from a task that merely has many locations.
deeper: The documented case: with many failing tests 'parallelization is trivial: each agent picks a different failing test to work on', but compiling the kernel was 'one giant task. Every agent would hit the same bug, fix that bug, and then overwrite each other's changes.'[^S5] The repair was a known-good oracle that split the work into per-file pieces.[^S5] This is one researcher's prototype, reported as observation rather than controlled comparison.
pitfall: Concluding that a stalled fan-out needs better prompts or more agents. When the task has one shared core, the repair is to change the task so it has seams.
distractor_rationale: Sixteen agents working hard looks like a system under load rather than a system colliding, since the symptom is zero throughput at full utilisation with no errors anywhere.

def: Several workers reaching the same underlying problem and overwriting each other's fixes.
pitfall: Looking for it in error logs. Nothing errors: each worker produces a reasonable change, and the damage is that the changes replace one another.
distractor_rationale: Concurrency bugs in ordinary software announce themselves with exceptions or corrupted state. Here every participant behaves correctly and the outcome is still wrong.

def: How much work a fan-out actually completes, as distinct from how busy its workers are.
pitfall: Inferring it from utilisation. The signature failure of an indivisible task is every worker fully occupied and almost nothing finished.
distractor_rationale: In most systems, high utilisation and high throughput move together, so busy workers read as productive ones.

def: Anything two workers use at the same time — an API quota, the filesystem, a git repository, a test runner, a database — through which independent tasks become one failure.
pitfall: Listing only what appears in the task description. The resources that take down a wave are the ones nobody wrote down: the model API, the gateway, the repository.
distractor_rationale: Independence is assessed against the task, because that is the object being decomposed. The execution path is a different object and is not represented anywhere in the plan.

def: A cap on API usage, applied across an organisation rather than per session, so every worker in a fan-out draws from one pool.
deeper: The documented mechanics: limits 'are set at the organization level', capacity is 'continuously replenished up to your maximum limit, rather than being reset at fixed intervals', and 'Short bursts of requests can exceed the limit and trigger rate limit errors.'[^S10]
pitfall: Reasoning about it as a total-work budget. Concurrency is a separate trigger: the same volume of work can pass steadily and fail as a burst.
distractor_rationale: A limit expressed per minute reads as an allowance to spend over that minute, and the token-bucket mechanics that make timing matter are not visible from the number.

def: The refill mechanism behind the rate limit: capacity is replenished continuously up to a maximum rather than reset at fixed intervals.
pitfall: Assuming a fresh allowance at the top of each minute. There is no reset moment to wait for; there is a level that refills as you spend, and a burst can drain it below zero regardless of the minute.
distractor_rationale: Most quotas people have dealt with — API calls per day, requests per hour — do reset on a boundary, so the mental model transfers and is wrong here.

def: A documented mechanism that returns 429 errors when an organisation's usage rises sharply, independently of the absolute volume.
pitfall: Trying to satisfy it by reducing total work. The trigger is the shape of the ramp: the documented advice is to 'ramp up your traffic gradually and maintain consistent usage patterns'.
distractor_rationale: Every other limit responds to using less, so the natural remedy is to shrink the job rather than to stagger its start.

def: How many workers run at the same instant, as distinct from how many pieces the task has.
pitfall: Setting it from the piece count. Ten pieces do not require ten simultaneous workers, and the choice between those is about blast radius and review capacity rather than about the decomposition.
distractor_rationale: Piece count is a fact about the task and concurrency is a decision about the run, but they are usually written down as the same number in the same breath.

def: One batch of workers dispatched together, after which results are collected before the next batch goes out.
pitfall: Treating waves as a compromise between serial and parallel. The first wave is a test of the brief at real cost, which is a distinct benefit neither pure shape provides.
distractor_rationale: On a speed axis, waves sit between the two extremes and look like a hedge. Their real advantage is on a different axis: they let the brief improve mid-run.

def: How many workers go out in one batch, chosen against how much can be lost in one failure and how much output can be reviewed at once.
pitfall: Choosing it for speed. The published operating point of three to five parallel subagents is small for reasons that survive across settings, and a brief that is wrong is wrong in every worker of the wave simultaneously.
distractor_rationale: Larger waves finish sooner in the success case, and the success case is the one people plan for.

def: The initial small batch, run deliberately before the rest, because it is the only real test of a brief.
pitfall: Skipping it when the brief looks solid. A brief reads correctly to its author by construction; the first wave is what reads it as a worker does.
distractor_rationale: Testing feels like a step for uncertain plans, and a carefully written brief does not feel uncertain. The defects it catches are ones invisible from the author's side.

def: How much is lost or left half-finished when a run fails — one piece in a serial run, an entire wave in a parallel one.
deeper: The documented distinction matters for diagnosis: a 500 is 'an unexpected error... internal to Anthropic's systems' with the guidance to 'Retry the request with exponential backoff', while a 429 is a rate limit carrying a retry-after header.[^S11]
pitfall: Weighing only the probability of failure. Partial states are worse than failures: each worker had written some output and not the rest, with no record of what completed.
distractor_rationale: Risk gets reasoned about as likelihood because that is what the word suggests, while the recovery cost is what actually differs between the dispatch shapes.

def: What a failed wave leaves behind: several workers having written some of their output and not the rest, with no record of who finished.
pitfall: Planning only for success and failure. The common outcome is neither, and recovery requires knowing which pieces completed — which nothing records unless each worker writes a completion marker as its last action.
distractor_rationale: A task is mentally binary: it worked or it did not. Agents write incrementally, so interruption lands between those states by default.

def: The response header a rate-limited request returns, indicating how long to wait — present on a 429 and absent from a server-side 500.
pitfall: Reading every failed request as a rate limit. The status code and the presence of this header distinguish a quota problem, which serialising fixes, from a server-side fault, which retrying with backoff addresses.
distractor_rationale: Both failures show up mid-run as a dead worker, and the immediate reaction is to reduce load — which is right for one cause and irrelevant to the other.

def: A lead waiting for all dispatched workers to finish before proceeding, which is the documented default.
deeper: The published account: 'our lead agents execute subagents synchronously, waiting for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding. This simplifies coordination, but creates bottlenecks in the information flow between agents.'[^S1]
pitfall: Sizing briefs for the average worker. A blocking wave runs at the speed of its slowest member, so an unbounded piece among bounded ones sets the clock for all of them.
distractor_rationale: The mean is the natural summary of a set of durations, and the tail only becomes salient after a wave has been held up by one worker.

def: Letting workers run and report without the lead waiting, at the price of harder coordination.
pitfall: Reaching for it to fix a slow wave. The named costs are 'result coordination, state consistency, and error propagation across the subagents', all of which land on you rather than on the tool.
distractor_rationale: It is the obvious answer to a blocking bottleneck, and its costs are the kind that only appear once something goes wrong mid-run.

def: The instruction governing the run as a whole, distinct from any worker's brief: how to divide the work, whether to wait, and what to return.
pitfall: Folding it into the briefs. The waiting decision and the no-merge instruction are properties of the run, and a worker cannot carry them because it does not know the other workers exist.
distractor_rationale: Everything reaching an agent arrives as text, so the boundary between per-worker and per-run instructions is not enforced by anything and is easy to lose.

def: Work whose main effect is modifying files, and the case documentation flags for conflicts when run in parallel.
pitfall: Running a first fan-out on it. Parallel edits combine two hard problems — coordinating writers and reviewing several diffs at once — and neither is where to learn the pattern.
distractor_rationale: Writing tasks are where the time is actually spent, so they are what people most want to parallelise first.

def: The document that turns several worker reports into one answer, and the last step where a claim can enter without anything checking it.
pitfall: Treating it as assembly. It is a generation pass over material nobody re-read, performed by an agent with no access to the underlying artifacts.
distractor_rationale: The inputs are already written, so the step feels editorial. Nothing about it is: the output contains sentences that were in none of the inputs.

def: The agent that reads the worker reports and produces the combined answer, with no access to anything the reports describe.
pitfall: Expecting it to catch a wrong finding. It cannot see the files, so a report that is confidently wrong is indistinguishable to it from one that is right.
distractor_rationale: It is the last stage and sees the most material, which reads as the position with the best overview. It has the best overview of the reports and no view of the work.

def: The task of producing one summary from several documents — structurally the synthesiser's job, and a task with measured hallucination behaviour.
deeper: The measured finding: 'on average, up to 75% of the content in LLM-generated summary is hallucinated, with hallucinations more likely to occur towards the end of the summaries', and when asked about topics that were not present, models 'still generate summaries about 79.35% and 44% of the time'.[^S13]
pitfall: Reading the measured rates as applying unchanged to your fan-out. The 75% upper bound comes from benchmarks built to surface the behaviour, on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o-era models; the mechanism generalises and the rate does not.
distractor_rationale: The figure is dramatic and easy to carry, and its setting is the part that gets dropped when it is repeated.

def: Whether a summary's claims are actually supported by its source material, as opposed to being fluent and plausible.
pitfall: Judging it by how well the synthesis reads. Fluency and faithfulness are independent, and the smoothest formulation is often the one that reconciled a real disagreement out of existence.
distractor_rationale: Readability is the only property visible without going back to the sources, so it becomes the proxy by default.

def: The measured tendency for where material sits in the input to change how faithfully it is represented in the output.
deeper: The measured shape: a 'U-shaped' trend in faithfulness where models 'faithfully summarize the beginning and end of documents but neglect middle content', and perturbing document order shows 'models are less faithful when important documents are placed in the middle of the input'.[^S14]
pitfall: Assuming reports get equal treatment because they are equally short and equally formatted. Position affects the result independently of content.
distractor_rationale: In a set of similar-looking inputs there is no visible reason for one to be favoured, so equal treatment is the natural assumption.

def: The observed pattern where faithfulness is highest at the beginning and end of the input and lowest in the middle.
pitfall: Treating it as a property of long inputs only. It was observed across long-form summarisation and it is the reason the report in the middle of a pile of six is the one most likely to be misrepresented.
distractor_rationale: It is usually encountered as a long-context phenomenon, which suggests a length threshold below which it does not apply.

def: Summarising each document separately and then iteratively merging the summaries — a structural approach measured to hurt faithfulness rather than help it.
deeper: The reported finding: 'Performing methods that changes the input structure (i.e., hierarchical merging or incremental updating) hurts faithfulness', while prompting to direct attention was 'moderately effective'.[^S14]
pitfall: Reaching for it when a synthesis comes out muddy. Adding a merging layer was tested against simple prompting and performed worse across all datasets.
distractor_rationale: More structure looks like more rigour, and the failure being addressed does look like an information-organisation problem.

def: Keeping a running summary and folding in one document at a time, which measurably trades one positional bias for another.
pitfall: Adopting it to avoid overloading the synthesiser. The measured result is that the model 'either retains its current summary and thus remains faithful to the first document or focuses on the last document', which is recency bias in place of lost-in-the-middle.
distractor_rationale: Processing one document at a time is a sound engineering instinct for anything memory-bound, and it fails here for a reason that has nothing to do with capacity.

def: Over-weighting the most recently seen material, which is what incremental merging produces in place of the bias it was meant to fix.
pitfall: Believing the fix worked because middle content is no longer being dropped. It is not being dropped from the middle any more because the whole output now tracks the last input.
distractor_rationale: The original symptom disappears, which is the usual evidence that a fix worked. The replacement failure has a different shape and is not being looked for.

def: A synthesis claim the author checked against the artifact personally, recorded with what was run or opened.
pitfall: Marking a claim verified because it is obviously right. Verified means you went and looked, and a claim you are confident about but did not check is reported.
distractor_rationale: Confidence and verification feel like the same state from inside, especially for claims that match what you already expected to find.

def: A synthesis claim that rests on one worker's assertion, attributed to that worker and left unverified.
pitfall: Stating it flatly. Attribution is what lets a reader weigh it, and an unattributed worker claim reads exactly like something you confirmed.
distractor_rationale: Attribution feels like hedging in a document meant to give an answer, so the attributive phrase is the first thing edited out for readability.

def: A synthesis category for claims where workers disagree, kept as a disagreement rather than resolved.
pitfall: Treating it as untidiness to clean up. Two workers differing usually means they defined the question differently, which is information about the task available no other way.
distractor_rationale: A report containing contradictions reads as unfinished, and resolving contradictions is what a synthesis appears to be for.

def: A synthesis claim the synthesiser produced that no worker made, marked as such so it cannot pass as a finding.
pitfall: Failing to notice them. An unmarked inference has the same voice, confidence, and sentence shape as a verified fact, and they cluster in the recommendation at the end.
distractor_rationale: Inferences are usually reasonable, which is precisely why they survive review — the test people apply is plausibility, and plausibility is what they have.

def: What happens when a synthesiser resolves a disagreement by producing a formulation that accommodates both sides, manufacturing a claim neither worker made.
pitfall: Being unable to detect it after the fact. A smoothed synthesis contains no trace of the smoothing; the only way to find it is to open every report a multi-worker claim covers.
distractor_rationale: The result reads better than either original, since accommodating both positions produces a more general and more confident sentence.

def: A worker's report that it finished — wrote the file, ran the tests, passed the checks — which is produced by the same process that did the work.
deeper: The same risk is named from the other side in an autonomous build: 'For autonomous systems, it is easy to see tests pass and assume the job is done, when this is rarely the case.'[^S5] The two incidents above are single observations from one build, not a general rate.
pitfall: Treating it as evidence that the work happened. In this course's own build, a worker reported 'file written, both validators pass' for a file that did not exist, and another reported a path that did not exist; both were caught only because the orchestrator re-ran the checks itself.
distractor_rationale: Completion claims are specific and checkable-sounding, and specificity reads as reliability. Nothing about being specific makes a claim true.

def: Checking a claim against the artifact rather than against the report — running the test yourself, listing the file, opening the path.
deeper: Verification is where the measured population breaks and where intervention moved the number: adding 'a high-level task objective verification step' produced a '+15.6% improvement in task success on ProgramDev'.[^S4] Those figures come from research frameworks on older models.
pitfall: Skipping it when the reports look consistent. Six workers can all report success and one of them can be describing a file that does not exist; consistency across reports says nothing about whether work happened.
distractor_rationale: Agreement between independent sources is strong evidence in most settings. Here the sources are not independent of the thing in question — each is reporting on itself.

def: Verification that confirms something cheap and adjacent — the code compiles, no TODOs remain — instead of whether the objective was met.
pitfall: Counting a check as verification because it ran and passed. The documented pattern is verifiers doing exactly this despite being prompted to be thorough.
distractor_rationale: A passing check produces a green result, which is the same signal a real verification produces. Nothing in the signal distinguishes what was checked.

def: An agent separated from the one that did the work, whose job is to judge it — the one structural intervention with first-party evidence behind it.
deeper: The reported experience: 'Out of the box, Claude is a poor QA agent. In early runs, I watched it identify legitimate issues, then talk itself into deciding they weren't a big deal and approve the work anyway.'[^S6]
pitfall: Expecting the separation alone to produce skepticism. The evaluator 'is still an LLM that is inclined to be generous towards LLM-generated outputs'; what separation buys is that tuning it to be skeptical is tractable.
distractor_rationale: The problem is framed as self-assessment bias, so removing the self appears to remove the bias. It removes the structural obstacle to fixing it, which is a smaller and more useful claim.

def: The agent producing the work in a generator-evaluator pair, as distinct from the one judging it.
pitfall: Asking it to grade its own output as a final step. Agents 'tend to respond by confidently praising the work - even when, to a human observer, the quality is obviously mediocre'.
distractor_rationale: A self-check costs one extra turn and produces a review-shaped response, so it looks like verification at a bargain price.

def: Splitting the agent that does the work from the agent that judges it, so the judgment does not run on the same process that produced the thing being judged.
pitfall: Reading it as sufficient rather than as an enabling condition. It is described as 'a strong lever' that does not 'immediately eliminate that leniency on its own'.
distractor_rationale: It is presented in the source as the fix for self-evaluation, and the qualification arrives in the following sentence, which is easy to read past.

def: A durable output on disk — a file, a commit, a written schema — as distinct from a claim in a report about it.
pitfall: Accepting a report's description of an artifact in place of the artifact. The distinction only matters when they differ, which is exactly when nothing else will catch it.
distractor_rationale: Reports describe artifacts accurately most of the time, so the description functions as a reliable proxy until the one case where it does not.

def: Verifying a sample of a report's claims — a few references, one count, one negative finding — to calibrate how much the rest can be trusted.
pitfall: Sampling only the claims that sound uncertain. The confident, specific ones are the ones nobody checks, and specificity is not evidence of having happened.
distractor_rationale: Attention is naturally drawn to whatever reads as shaky, which is a reasonable triage heuristic everywhere except where the signal has no relationship to accuracy.

def: The section of a synthesis recording what went wrong, what was re-run, what was sampled, and what the run cost — the part that lets a reader weigh everything above it.
deeper: The reasoning behind reporting configuration generalises from eval practice, where undocumented setup makes results hard to interpret: 'collapsing them into a single score without specifying the resource configuration makes the differences - and real-world generalizability - hard to interpret.'[^S15]
pitfall: Omitting it to keep the document clean. Without it a reader cannot tell a spot-checked reference from an unchecked one, or a corrected brief from a uniform run, and has to ask you.
distractor_rationale: It makes the work look less clean, and a synthesis is usually written to be persuasive as well as accurate.

def: One dispatch of several workers from a single lead, and the unit at which concurrency risk is actually taken.
pitfall: Sizing it from the piece count instead of from blast radius and review capacity. In this course's own build, five independent workers dispatched at once all failed together against one shared gateway, and the same five tasks succeeded run one at a time.
distractor_rationale: The number of pieces is a concrete fact about the task and the two constraints that should decide the size are judgments, so the concrete number wins by default.
